title: #1 Hypnotism Expert: “Your Personality is a Trance, Do This to Wake Up” | Dr. David Spiegel
author: Dr. David Spiegel
summary: Argues that personality is a convenient assumption rather than a fixed fact, and that hypnosis is a fast, measurable way to demonstrate it. Spiegel, a Stanford psychiatrist, defines hypnosis as a state of highly focused attention with three signatures visible on fMRI: reduced activity in the dorsal anterior cingulate (the brain's alarm system, so less distraction), increased connectivity between prefrontal cortex and the insula (a stronger mind-body channel), and decreased connectivity to the posterior cingulate and default mode network — the circuit that guards your assumptions about who you are. Loosening that third connection is what lets someone try out being different. He argues this makes hypnosis purpose-driven and quick where meditation is open presence, and reframes trauma-related self-blame as a false bid for control: we would rather feel guilty than helpless.
takeaways: Hypnosis is defined as highly focused attention — the state of being so absorbed in a film you forget you are watching one — not a loss of will. Spiegel has hypnotised 11,000 people and formally scored 7,000 on his 0-10 profile.

Three fMRI signatures: dorsal anterior cingulate activity drops (less distraction), prefrontal–insula connectivity rises (mind-body conduit), and connectivity to the posterior cingulate falls, disconnecting you from the default mode network's account of who you ought to be.
He nicknames the default mode network 'the my fault mode network' — useful for self-constancy, but also where irrational beliefs and inherited expectations keep you on track.

Hypnotisability is a stable trait, as stable as IQ by your early twenties: a Stanford study blind-retested former psych-one students after 25 years and found a .7 correlation between scores at 20 and at 50.
Most children are highly hypnotisable and lose it in adolescence, when formal operations arrive and you 'begin to favor logic over experience'.

Somatosensory evoked-response study: hypnotic suggestion of cold, numb hands halved the response amplitude and made the P100 wave disappear within a tenth of a second — perception modulated at the neural level, not just self-report.
PET study with coloured and black-and-white grids: suggesting the colour drain away changed activity in the lingual gyrus, the visual colour-processing region, in the corresponding direction.

Hypnotisability has a biological component: a variant of the catechol-O-methyltransferase gene metabolising dopamine at a middling rate, plus cerebrospinal levels of the dopamine metabolite homovanillic acid, both correlate with it. Childhood abuse also raises it, via dissociation as escape.
One in four smokers stop after a single session using the reframe: smoking is a poison, I need my body to live, I owe my body respect and protection.

Historical note: Mesmer was investigated by a French panel including Benjamin Franklin, Lavoisier and Dr Guillotin, who concluded hypnosis was 'nothing but heated imagination' — a definition Spiegel rather likes.

The practical inversion: start 'from the body up rather than the head down'. Psychiatry usually works out the problem first and expects relief to follow; hypnosis settles the body first so you can then think clearly, breaking the snowball of physical tension feeding mental stress.

Performance work is process over outcome: Zen archers say the problem is focusing on the target rather than the bow and arrow — get the relationship with the instrument right and the arrow lands. Used with golfers and the Stanford women's swim team, who were swimming faster in practice than in meets.
Memory is laid down with emotion attached, not painted on afterwards: 'affect colors memory and memory colors affect' — which is both the problem and the opening for change.
quotes: Your personality. It's just a convenient assumption. We are a lot more tangible than we imagine.
Trauma is making a person into an object, a thing, and you lose agency... And we would rather feel guilty than helpless.
It kind of preserves your assumptions and expectations about who you are and what you are... I sometimes call it the my fault mode network.
It helps you to to regulate who you want to be, not just who you are... make it a a system that you use, but not a system that uses you.
So affect colors memory and memory colors affect.
Teach people how to start out from the body up rather than the head down.
The problem with most archers is that they focus on the target, not the bow and arrow.
bestIdeas: Guilt as a disguised bid for control. If believing you could have prevented something is preferable to accepting you were helpless, then self-blame is doing a job — and the intervention is to name that job, not to argue with the belief.
The self-model is a brain circuit you can turn down. Treating identity as maintained machinery rather than fact reframes 'trying out being different' as a mechanical possibility, not a metaphor.
Purpose-driven versus open presence. His distinction between hypnosis and meditation is a useful general filter: is this practice for changing something specific, or for being with whatever arises?
Match the intervention to the trait. He scores hypnotisability first because highs and lows need different approaches — the same instruction produces different results depending on measured capacity.
Change can be fast. Decades of therapy versus a single reframing question is an argument that duration is not the measure of depth, when the intervention meets the actual mechanism.
Body before cognition. Reversing the usual order — regulate the physical response first, then reason about the problem — is a general anxiety move that needs no hypnosis to apply.
The split screen: one stressor on one side, one thing you could do about it on the other, and only one of each. A constraint that forces triage where rumination would otherwise sprawl.
tools: Hypnotic Induction Profile — Spiegel's clinical 0-10 hypnotisability scale, administered in five or six minutes.
The eye-roll sign — the upward eye-roll marker developed by his father, Herbert Spiegel, correlating with hypnotisability.
fMRI, PET and somatosensory evoked-response EEG — the imaging methods behind the mechanism and perception studies.
Reverie — the self-hypnosis app Spiegel co-founded to make the method broadly available (the captions render it 'Rey' and 'Revery').
Zen in the Art of Archery — the book behind the target-versus-bow-and-arrow framing of process over outcome.
method: Look at the examiner, then look up toward the top of your head, keeping the head level.
Keep looking up and slowly close your eyes; take a deep breath and let it out slowly through the mouth.
Let the eyes relax while staying closed, and let the body float — a bath, a lake, a hot tub, or space.
The examiner strokes the middle finger of the left hand, suggesting tingling, numbness and lightness, and the forearm floats up as if magnetically pulled.
The hand is instructed to stay light and upright even after the eyes open, and to float back up if pushed down.
A touch to the left elbow returns normal sensation and control.
Come out by counting backwards: on three get ready, on two roll the eyes up behind closed lids, on one let the eyes open.
Score by asking what the hand feels and whether it seems less a part of the body than the other — the degree of dissociation is the measure.
Stress protocol, distinct from the induction above: look up, close the eyes, deep breath, and float somewhere comfortable — get the body settled FIRST.
Then picture a pleasant scene on an imaginary screen to reinforce that physical comfort.
Divide the screen in half: on one side one stressor — one, not twelve — while the body stays comfortable; on the other side one thing you could do about it, not necessarily the best or only thing.

keyMessage: Personality is a convenient assumption maintained by a specific brain circuit, so it can be turned down and tried differently — the aim is a self you use rather than one that uses you.
